label: 4QMMT (Some Works of the Torah) — Complete
summary_plain: 4QMMT is a letter from the Qumran community to the Jerusalem establishment listing specific legal disagreements. The letter begins with a calendar section establishing a 364-day solar calendar. It then lists approximately twenty halakhic rulings where the community disagrees with the Temple authorities — matters of purity, sacrifice, and priestly conduct. The letter concludes with a plea: we have separated ourselves from the majority of the people because of these matters. Consider the blessings and curses that came upon the kings of Yisra'el. We have written to you so that you may understand the book of Moshe.
summary_scholarly: 4QMMT (Miqtsat Ma'ase HaTorah — 'Some Works of the Torah') was reconstructed from six Cave 4 manuscripts (4Q394-4Q399). It is a sectarian halakhic letter — the only known direct correspondence from the Qumran community to the Jerusalem religious establishment. The text is divided into three sections: a 364-day solar calendar (Section A), a list of approximately twenty legal disputes (Section B), and an exhortation citing the blessings and curses of the Torah (Section C). The halakhic disputes concern purity laws, sacrifice, and calendar. The letter documents the moment of sectarian separation: the community separated because the Temple authorities followed incorrect rulings.

key_terms.definition: Hebrew for 'Some Works of the Torah' — the formal title of 4QMMT. The phrase refers to specific legal rulings derived from the Torah of Moshe that the Qumran community considered binding and that the Jerusalem establishment was violating.

The calendar used by the Qumran community, documented in Section A of 4QMMT, Yovelim, and 1 Chanokh. Divides the year into four seasons of 91 days. Festivals always fall on the same weekday. The primary calendar dispute between Qumran and the Jerusalem Temple.
Legal ruling derived from Torah; 4QMMT contains approximately twenty specific halakhic disputes (Section B) where the community's ruling differs from the Jerusalem Temple's practice.

Separation — the act of the Qumran community separating from the majority. 'We have separated ourselves from the majority of the people.' The document's central claim justifying the community's existence as a separate covenant entity.
Seasonal marker — the 364-day calendar divides into four tekufot (seasons) of 91 days each, ensuring feast days never fall on certain days that would create purity conflicts.

The approximately twenty specific legal rulings in 4QMMT where the Qumran community disagrees with the Jerusalem establishment: purity of liquid streams, skin disease purity, Gentile grain offerings, dog bones in Jerusalem, and others.
Blessings and curses — Section C of 4QMMT appeals to the blessings and curses in the Torah (Devarim 28) as the consequence framework for following or rejecting YHWH's rulings.

The six Cave 4 manuscript designations from which 4QMMT was reconstructed by scholars. No single complete copy survived — the full text required combining overlapping fragments from six separate copies.
Kings cited in Section C of 4QMMT as examples of rulers who either followed or deviated from YHWH's Torah, with consequences. The letter uses them as a warning to the Jerusalem leadership.

One of the disputed rulings in Section B: whether a liquid stream poured from a clean vessel into an unclean one transfers impurity upward. The Qumran ruling: yes, it does. The Jerusalem Temple ruling: no. A specific example of the kind of technical purity debate documented in 4QMMT.

faq.question: What does the calendar dispute in 4QMMT reveal about the Great Eraser?
faq.answer: 4QMMT documents that the Qumran community observed a 364-day solar calendar — the same calendar prescribed in Yovelim and 1 Chanokh. The Jerusalem Temple used a different lunar calendar. This meant the two groups celebrated festivals on different days. The community considered this worth separating over. The solar calendar was eventually suppressed entirely — the Rabbinic tradition that survived after 70 CE adopted the lunar calendar exclusively. The 364-day calendar preserved at Qumran was erased from mainstream practice. The Great Eraser operates through calendar substitution: change when a people worship and you change who they are.

faq.question: Why is 4QMMT significant for understanding sectarian separation?
faq.answer: 4QMMT is the only known letter from the Qumran community to the Jerusalem establishment. It does not argue theology in the abstract. It lists specific legal rulings — approximately twenty — where the community disagrees with the Temple authorities. These are concrete disputes: purity of liquid streams, handling of skin disease, which animals may be sacrificed, whether Gentile grain offerings are permissible. The letter concludes by citing the blessings and curses of the Torah, warning the Jerusalem leaders to reconsider. The separation was not foreign persecution — the institutional gatekeepers of the Temple were themselves, in this community's judgment, violating the Torah.

faq.question: What is Section A of 4QMMT about?
faq.answer: Section A establishes the 364-day solar calendar — a year of four seasons of 91 days each, with festivals always falling on fixed weekdays. This is the same calendar documented in 1 Chanokh (the Astronomical Book) and in Yovelim (Jubilees). The placement of the calendar at the top of the letter signals that the calendar dispute was the foundational disagreement — wrong calendar, wrong festivals, wrong covenant observance.

faq.question: What is Section B of 4QMMT?
faq.answer: Section B lists approximately twenty specific halakhic (legal) rulings where the Qumran community's reading of Torah differs from the Jerusalem Temple's practice. The disputes are technical and precise: purity of liquid streams poured between vessels; treatment of skin disease; handling of grain offerings from Gentiles; dog bones in the city of the Temple; and others. These are not minor preferences — the community considered the Temple's rulings violations of the Torah of Moshe.

faq.question: What is Section C of 4QMMT?
faq.answer: Section C is a concluding exhortation. It appeals to the blessings and curses in the Torah (rooted in Devarim 28), citing the history of the kings of Yisra'el as evidence: those who obeyed YHWH's Torah were delivered from troubles; those who did not were brought under the curses. The letter closes: 'We have written to you so that you may understand the book of Moshe.' This is an appeal, not a declaration of war — the community still believed the Jerusalem leadership could be persuaded.

faq.question: Why was the purity of liquid streams a significant dispute?
faq.answer: The question was whether a liquid stream poured from a clean vessel into an impure one transfers impurity back up the stream to the clean vessel. The Qumran community said yes — the impurity travels upward through the stream. The Jerusalem Temple authorities said no. This seems minor but it had real consequences for Temple practice: if impurity travels up a liquid stream, entire processes of sacrificial preparation could be compromised. It illustrates how the disputes in 4QMMT are not about abstract theology but about the practical mechanics of covenant observance.

faq.question: How was 4QMMT reconstructed?
faq.answer: No single complete copy of 4QMMT survived. The text was reconstructed by combining overlapping fragments from six different Cave 4 manuscripts (4Q394 through 4Q399). Each copy was fragmentary. By identifying overlapping passages and aligning them, scholars established the complete structure: Section A (calendar), Section B (halakhic disputes), Section C (exhortation). The reconstruction confirms that 4QMMT was copied multiple times — suggesting it was important enough to preserve in multiple copies across the community.

faq.question: Does 4QMMT mention the Teacher of Righteousness?
faq.answer: 4QMMT does not name the Teacher of Righteousness directly in the surviving text. However, scholars widely regard it as either written by or closely associated with the Teacher, based on its first-person plural voice ('we have separated ourselves'), its tone of authoritative legal instruction, and its position as the founding document of the separation from Jerusalem. It may be the letter that precipitated the founding of the Qumran community as a separate entity.

faq.question: What is the connection between 4QMMT and the Damascus Document?
faq.answer: Both texts document the same separation — the Qumran community's break from the Jerusalem establishment — but from different angles. 4QMMT presents the legal case: here are the specific rulings you are getting wrong. The Damascus Document (CD) presents the theological and historical case: we are the Plant Root, the remnant of the covenant, following the Teacher of Righteousness. Together they form the founding documents of the sect: the legal rationale (4QMMT) and the narrative identity (Damascus Document).

faq.question: What does 4QMMT tell us about the relationship between the Qumran community and the Jerusalem Temple?
faq.answer: 4QMMT reveals that the community had not yet fully abandoned hope of convincing the Jerusalem establishment. The tone is persuasive, not denunciatory. They wrote the letter; they cited Torah; they appealed to historical examples. This suggests the final break — the full settlement at Qumran — may have come after the letter was ignored. The Damascus Document's harsher language ('the Man of the Lie', 'the Wicked Priest') likely reflects the later, hardened position after the persuasion attempt of 4QMMT failed.

faq.question: Why does the community appeal specifically to the kings of Yisra'el in Section C?
faq.answer: Because the kings are the clearest historical record of the Torah's covenant consequences playing out in real time. The kings who kept YHWH's Torah survived and flourished; those who abandoned it brought destruction on themselves and the people. By invoking this pattern, 4QMMT's Section C is not merely quoting history — it is warning the Jerusalem leaders that they are on the same path as the kings who brought the first exile. The appeal carries the weight of Devarim 28's covenant curse framework.
